interviewQuestions.question: How would you delete a node with two children from a BST while keeping the tree valid?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The zero- and one-child cases are simple — remove the node and splice up whatever child exists, if any. The two-child case is the real problem: I can't just remove the node, because both children need somewhere valid to go, and neither can simply inherit the parent's slot without breaking the ordering for the other subtree.

The standard fix: find the node's **inorder successor** — the smallest value in its right subtree, reached by walking left from the right child until there's no more left to go. Copy that successor's value into the node being "deleted" (so the node keeps its position but takes on the successor's value), then actually delete the successor node itself from its original location.

What makes this safe: the successor, by construction, can never have a left child — if it did, that child would be even smaller, and the successor wouldn't have been the smallest value found by walking left. So deleting the successor always reduces to one of the two easy cases, never back to a two-child problem. And copying its value up preserves the BST invariant automatically, since the successor was already confirmed to be the smallest value strictly greater than the original node.

I'd also mention the inorder **predecessor** — the largest value in the left subtree — works symmetrically and is an equally valid choice; picking one consistently is what matters, not which one specifically.

**Testing:** whether you can justify why the successor swap preserves the invariant, not just recite the steps.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Deletion

interviewQuestions.question: How would you validate that a binary tree satisfies the BST property, and what's the common mistake people make?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The common mistake is checking each node only against its immediate parent — comparing a node's value to its parent's and calling it valid if the local ordering looks right. That misses the actual invariant, which constrains a node's relationship to its **entire** ancestor chain, not just the one node directly above it. A tree can have every single parent-child pair individually well-ordered while still containing a violation several levels up — for instance, a left child could correctly be smaller than its immediate parent but larger than an ancestor two levels above that, which a parent-only check simply never examines.

The correct approach carries a valid **range** down through the recursion: start with (-infinity, infinity) at the root, and each time you go left, tighten the upper bound to the current node's value; each time you go right, tighten the lower bound. A node fails validation the moment its value falls outside the range accumulated from every ancestor on its path, not just its parent.

An equally correct alternative that avoids explicit range-tracking: run an inorder traversal and check the output is strictly increasing, since a BST's inorder traversal is sorted if and only if the whole tree is valid — this is arguably simpler to reason about, at the cost of building the full traversal rather than validating in a single top-down pass.

**Testing:** whether you catch that the invariant is about the whole ancestor chain, a subtle but common validation bug.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Validation

interviewQuestions.question: Why would search and insert on a BST silently degrade from O(log n) to O(n), and what would you do about it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
A plain BST's height depends entirely on insertion order, and there's no guarantee baked in that it stays balanced. Inserting already-sorted (or reverse-sorted) data is the worst case: every new value is larger than everything currently in the tree, so each insertion becomes the current rightmost node's only child, building a straight chain rather than a branching structure. That chain has height O(n), and since search, insert, and delete are all O(height), they all silently become O(n) — with no crash, no exception, just a correct program that's unexpectedly slow.

This is a genuinely realistic production scenario, not just a contrived interview edge case — data arriving in sorted order (timestamps, auto-incrementing IDs, alphabetically pre-sorted input) is common, and a naive BST built from it is pathologically bad by construction, exactly when it looks like it should be fine.

The fix is a **self-balancing** tree — AVL or red-black — which enforces a height invariant on every insert and delete via rotations, guaranteeing O(log n) height regardless of insertion order. In practice, I'd reach for a language's built-in ordered structure (`TreeMap` in Java, `std::map` in C++), which is red-black under the hood, rather than hand-rolling balancing logic, unless the interview is specifically asking me to implement it.

**Testing:** whether you recognize that a correct-looking BST can have a hidden, realistic performance cliff, and know the standard fix.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Performance

interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose a balanced BST over a hash map, given that the hash map has faster average-case search?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Purely on raw search speed, a hash map usually wins — O(1) average versus a BST's O(log n). But that comparison is incomplete, because a hash map gives up something a BST keeps: **ordering**. There's no efficient way to ask a hash map for "the next value greater than x," "all values between x and y," or "iterate everything in sorted order" — none of that is supported at all, let alone efficiently.

A balanced BST answers all of those in O(log n) or O(log n + k) for a range of size k, while still supporting O(log n) insert and delete — meaningfully better than a sorted array's O(n) insert, which is the other structure that preserves ordering.

So the decision comes down to what the workload actually needs: if it's pure point lookups with no ordering requirement, a hash map is usually the better default. The moment a problem needs range queries, nearest-neighbor-style lookups (floor/ceiling), or sorted iteration alongside mutation, a balanced BST — or a library's ordered map type built on one — becomes the right tool, even though it gives up the hash map's raw lookup speed to get there.

I'd frame this as reading the actual requirement rather than defaulting to "hash map is always fastest" — it's fastest for one specific operation, not for everything a data structure might need to do.

**Testing:** whether you evaluate structures against the full set of operations a problem needs, not a single benchmark number.
